Leonardo, it is Richard, from the fund. Quick voice note before tomorrow, so that we do not waste the twenty minutes. First, keep the opening to two minutes. Give me the agenda, then go straight into the numbers. I do not need the history of the reform, I read the memo. Second, the fifteen percent. I know you cannot confirm it before the ruling, and honestly I am not expecting a final number tomorrow. Give me the range, and tell me what the range depends on. If you say fifteen and it becomes twenty-two, that is the end of the relationship, so please hedge it properly. Third, Margaret will push you. She always does. Do not invent an answer, just tell her when you will come back with it. And at the end of the call, I want one page in writing, with the next steps and a date on each one. That is all. Talk tomorrow.

The first time I ran a meeting with a client this size, I sat there and waited to be asked. Nobody asked. Somebody else opened, somebody else set the agenda, and by minute four the room belonged to them. That is the whole lesson, and it took me years to learn it. Three sentences changed my career. The first one is the opening: let me take you through the agenda. You say that in the first thirty seconds and the room is yours. The second one is for the moment you do not know: let me look into that and come back to you on Thursday. Not knowing is normal in advisory work. Disappearing is not. And the third one is the last minute of every meeting, which most people waste on small talk. I repeat the next steps out loud, who does what and by when. If you do only that, people will remember you as the person who runs a good meeting, even on the days when the numbers are bad.
